extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural historians, students of architecture, and educated readers interested in Venetian medieval architecture and conservation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative observatory criteria and aesthetic/technical principles for assessing early Venetian church architecture (here, Murano / San Donato): proportion, materiality, ornament, structural adaptations, and preservation. The page mixes measured description with prescriptive aesthetic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional harmony / arithmetic proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: The relations of the sides and internal spaces are in strict arithmetic proportion (e.g., interval of shafts 8'2", width of aisle 16'4", width of transept 24'6", width of nave 32'8") and such precise ratios are signs of aesthetic success: 'the proportions above given... might have been dictated by a mere love of mathematical precision; but those of the apse could only have resulted from a true love of harmony.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate plan and elevation by measured ratios and numerical relationships. Exact, repeated proportions (simple multiples/arithmetical sequences) indicate intentional design and harmony. Use the recorded measurements as examples of desirable proportional systems; lack of coherent ratios signals loss of original design integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate subtle variations within proportion to create cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: Early builders intentionally introduced small alternating changes (e.g., 'diminution of two inches on a breadth of seven feet and a half') between elements to produce cadence and oppose monotony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether minor, consistent departures from strict uniformity are intentional design devices (rhythm/cadence) rather than random defects. Small, regular alternations are a positive aesthetic feature; irregular or accidental variations are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective ornamentation to preserve color purity and viewer attention
rubrics_metrics.description: 'They left their purple capitals full broad masses of color; and sculptured the white ones.' Carving colored (purple) marble would mix grey shadow with the hue and draw attention away from the color, so ornamentation was applied selectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge ornamentation choices by their effect on material color and visual focus. Prefer leaving richly colored stones uncarved to preserve chromatic impact and carving paler stones to provide sculptural interest. Anti-pattern: carving colored marbles in ways that adulterate hue or distract from intended color effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polychrome inlaid ornament and banded decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: A decorative band ('like a silver girdle') of sharp marble wedges inlaid in brickwork and a second band of triangular recesses form an important ornamental device; the lower band shows deliberate color arrangement and chequering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the presence, completeness, and color logic of inlaid bands and triangular inlays. The variety and placement of inlaid triangles (ten distinct kinds described) and their color chequering are markers of the original builder's care. Missing inlays may be judged as losses; surviving patterned bands are of high importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material allocation: structural vs decorative use of brick and stone
rubrics_metrics.description: The builder used yellow brick for parts requiring strength and a deep red, more porous brick chiefly for decoration; brick thickness varies (2–4 inches) and lengths can be large for important positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing construction, distinguish materials used for load-bearing versus decorative roles. Durable, compact yellow brick (or equivalent) should form structural elements; more porous/red bricks may be acceptable for decorative infill. Note variations in brick size as intentional technical choices rather than mere irregularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied marble palette and chequered color schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: A palette of marbles was used (pure white; white veined with purple; brecciated white/black; white/deep green; deep red like Egyptian porphyry; grey/black layered marble) to produce contrasts and jewel-like inlays in the decorative band.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess decorative schemes by the selection and juxtaposition of marble types and colors. Successful schemes use contrast and repetition (chequering) to create visual richness; evaluate surviving examples against the ten described triangle types and their placements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for original fabric; critique of destructive restorations
rubrics_metrics.description: The author emphasizes that 'the whole impression and effect of the building are irretrievably lost' in many cases, and values surviving ancient fragments as 'most precious.' He declines to trace destructive modern restorations, implying that such restorations often harm the original's integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize original, datable fabric when judging architectural quality. Treat modern restorations skeptically when they obscure or replace essential ancient features. Preservation of original fragments is a primary positive criterion; modernizing interventions that destroy original effect are an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural ingenuity via adapted classical elements (buttressing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The apse's stability is achieved by a system of buttresses obtained by adaptations of the Roman shaft and arch: thick lower wall with semicircular niches flanked by pairs of shafts forming massy buttresses topped by an open gallery and arches supporting the roof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate structural systems for intelligent adaptation of available elements (e.g., using shaft-and-arch compositions as buttresses). Prize solutions that combine structural efficacy with coherent aesthetic expression rather than crude applied buttresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured detail and empirical metrics as evidence of design intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Dimensions of shafts, piers, distances, and plans are given precisely (e.g., shafts ~5'4" circumference; main piers 4'7" by 3'6"); such measurement helps determine original form and intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful measurement to distinguish original design proportions from later alterations. Detailed metrics supply objective grounds for attributing work to certain periods and for assessing the coherence of the design system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric plan arrangement and expressive polygonal apse
rubrics_metrics.description: The apse is heptagonal externally, arranged in four magnitudes so that, if completed, the figure would have sixteen sides; the seven sides are arranged with the central one widest—an intentional geometric ordering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess plan geometry for deliberate polygonal ordering and hierarchical side magnitudes. Such geometric complexity reflects refined planning and should be regarded as a positive aesthetic-structural attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with natural light, reflections and setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of village towers 'poised apparently in the air' with vivid reflections, the burnished lagoon, and crystalline vermilion imply that the visual effect of architecture in its landscape and light is integral to its success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate buildings not only in isolated plan/elevation terms but by how they relate to light, water, and landscape. Successful architecture harmonizes with and exploits local atmospheric and reflective conditions; failures ignore context or produce discordant visual effects.
